documents: Kim, Bowman, Fee (2022), Finite-Difference Simulation for Infrasound Generated by Finite-Extent Ground Motions, Seismological Research Letters (LLNL-JRNL-831344 accepted manuscript, PDF)

entry.evidence: The effects of complex source geometry and its extent have not been extensively studied nor have they been evaluated with high-fidelity finite difference simulations.

sequences.source_document: Kim, Bowman, Fee (2022) SRL accepted manuscript PDF

steps.action: Pose the gap: finite-difference infrasound modelling treats sources as single points, and the effect of finite-extent source geometry has not been evaluated.
steps.quote: acoustic sources are often oversimplified as [...] .

steps.action: Take the Rayleigh integral, used by other groups for SPE and other surface-motion sources, as the existing expectation and note its restriction to planar, homogeneous media.
steps.quote: This method has been used to model infrasound generation and propagation from underground chemical explosions

steps.action: Derive a discretized distributed-point-source representation (mass flow rates from surface element volume changes) from the Rayleigh/Kirchhoff-Helmholtz integral for use in the ElAc finite-difference code.
steps.quote: This integral equation is theoretically equivalent to the pressure field generated by a continuous distribution of point sources on the surface

steps.action: Benchmark the finite-difference point-source solution for a 50 m baffled circular piston against a finely discretized numerical Rayleigh integral reference (max error 0.22% at 1 m grid).
steps.quote: We use this solution obtained by the numerical Rayleigh integral as a reference for comparison.

steps.action: Vary the finite-difference grid spacing (3.0 to 1.0 m, 10 to 28 points per wavelength) and report the maximum waveform error at each (4% at 10 ppw, below 1% at 15 ppw).
steps.quote: we run the finite-difference simulations with different grid spacings to evaluate the accuracy of the point source approach

steps.action: Retain the distributed point source representation as verified on the piston problem and carry it to field data.
steps.quote: the mathematical representation of distributed point sources was developed for surface motions and verified by a theoretical piston problem

steps.action: Use the SPE Phase I field experiment (SPE-6 shot) with its epicentral accelerometer network and eight acoustic arrays, collected by the SPE program, as the test conditions.
steps.quote: we use the data obtained from Source Physics Experiments (SPE) Phase I

steps.action: Process the twelve epicentral accelerograms: low-pass filter at 5 Hz and interpolate/extrapolate over 250 m x 250 m with radial basis functions at 5 m spacing to obtain surface motion fields showing spall.
steps.quote: the ground motions recorded on the accelerometer are low-pass filtered by a fourth-order Butterworth window function with a cutoff frequency at 5 Hz

steps.action: Configure the ElAc simulation: 2500 point sources at 5 m spacing (13.6 ppw, chosen from the piston result), 10 x 6 x 6 km domain, rigid ground with USGS DEM topography, GFS-derived vertically layered atmosphere smoothed over 70 m.
steps.quote: A total of 2500 point sources equivalent to the ground motions are placed over 250m x 250m epicentral region.

steps.action: Compute synthetic infrasound waveforms with ElAc (topography, homogeneous atmosphere) and with the Rayleigh integral (planar, homogeneous) from the same surface motions.
steps.quote: Synthetic acoustic signals are recorded at IS14, IS24, IS31, and IS42 (Figure 1) and compared with the field observations

steps.action: Compare ElAc synthetics with observed waveforms at 0.2 to 4.9 km; uplift, dwell and slapdown features are reproduced (Figure 6).
steps.quote: The prediction by ElAc (red line) shows remarkably good agreement with the observation

steps.action: Attribute remaining discrepancies to the sparse accelerometer interpolation of the source motion and to unmodelled seismic-to-acoustic conversions, rather than to the method.
steps.quote: The discrepancies between the prediction and observation should be partly attributed to the accuracy of the ground motions used for the simulations.

steps.action: Conclude that local SPE acoustic signals are a direct response to epicentral spall ground motion, as previously proposed.
steps.quote: Our simulation results confirm that the local acoustic signals recorded for SPE are governed by a direct response to the epicentral ground motions

steps.action: Check the ElAc distributed-source result against the Rayleigh integral on the same SPE-6 source; they do not noticeably differ given low relief, and both errors grow with distance, pointing to unmodelled atmosphere.
steps.quote: The ElAc results also show good agreement with the Rayleigh integral results

steps.action: Image the simulated wavefield in vertical cross sections and show strong vertical directionality from in-phase interference over the finite source (Figure 7a-b).
steps.quote: These wavefield images at different times show the development of a vertically directional infrasound wavefield for SPE-6.

steps.action: Compare 2 Hz amplitude directionality from ElAc and the Rayleigh integral (Figure 7c); no considerable difference.
steps.quote: the amplitudes of the Elac and Rayleigh integral do not show considerable difference in directionality.

steps.action: Rerun ElAc with a vertically layered GFS atmosphere instead of a homogeneous one, keeping topography and source fixed (Figure 8).
steps.quote: We performed another ElAc simulation with the same topography and source time functions, but this time the atmosphere was assumed to be vertically layered

steps.action: Compare both atmosphere runs with data: good fit to 1 km, but amplitudes overestimated at 2.0 and 4.9 km; layered atmosphere improves IS5-1 via upward refraction.
steps.quote: at Station IS7-1 (2.0km) and IS5-1 (4.9km), amplitude differences between the predictions and observation are obvious.

steps.action: Attribute the residual far-station amplitude error to the accuracy and resolution of the GFS weather model and near-surface turbulence rather than to the source method.
steps.quote: This prediction error can be largely attributed to the accuracy and resolution of the weather model used in the simulation.

steps.action: Keep the distributed point source method as validated on the piston problem and on SPE-6 field data, applicable in realistic topography and atmospheres.
steps.quote: The results demonstrated that the distributed point sources represented air volume changes produced by the ground motions resulting in remarkable agreement with observed infrasound waveforms.

tree.answer: Infrasound from non-compact, explosion-induced ground motion (spall) that a single point source may not capture
Ground motion and near-field infrasound observed directly at SPE-6; 3-D radiation pattern not observable, so simulated
Build and characterize a finite-difference source representation for finite-extent ground motion
No rival hypotheses; alternative methods are the single point source and the Rayleigh integral
ElAc and Rayleigh integral expected to differ only with pronounced topography; they did not differ at SPE-6
Conditions found: one SPE-6 field shot with existing instrumentation; synthetic piston conditions set computationally
Survives grid-spacing variation, comparison with Rayleigh integral, and atmosphere variation; far-station amplitude misfit remains
Kept: method characterized as accurate for near-field SPE-6 infrasound

end.claim: Distributed point sources derived from the Rayleigh integral and inserted in a finite-difference code reproduce the Rayleigh integral (errors below 1% at about 15 points per wavelength) and observed SPE-6 infrasound waveforms within about 1 km, while allowing topography and layered atmospheres.

decisive_move.sentence: The comparison of ElAc distributed-source synthetics with SPE-6 infrasound observations is what turns a verified numerical equivalence into a field-validated capability.

gates.evidence: The SPE data were collected by the SPE program before and independently of this method (p. 12, 20). The piston benchmark has a quantitative error metric that could have failed (p. 11-12), but the field comparison is qualitative with no stated threshold for agreement (p. 15-16, 18). The 5 m spacing is justified by the piston result (p. 14), but nothing is stated as fixed before the field data were seen; the 5 Hz cutoff was chosen from the observed signal content (p. 13).

imports.item: 6th-order summation-by-parts finite-difference scheme (Petersson and Sjogreen 2018) in ElAc
Radial basis function interpolation of scattered data (Morse et al. 2005, SIGGRAPH)

novelty_claims.quote: The effects of complex source geometry and its extent have not been extensively studied nor have they been evaluated with high-fidelity finite difference simulations.
SPE provides a unique dataset, including epicentral ground motion measurements, which can be used to derive distributed point sources.
this experiment provided a unique opportunity to derive equivalent point source distribution.

limits: Only one of six SPE shots (SPE-6) is used; no other event or site tests the method, so generalization to pronounced topography, earthquakes or landslides is asserted, not shown (p. 17-20). Field agreement is judged visually; no misfit statistic is reported for the SPE comparison. The topography advantage over the Rayleigh integral could not be demonstrated because SPE-6 relief is low (p. 16-17). Sub-claims: spall as the governor of local SPE infrasound is best_explanation, agreeing with cited work (p. 16); vertical directionality is a simulation result consistent with Blom et al. 2020, not observed (p. 17); attribution of far-station amplitude error to the weather model is best_explanation, untested (p. 19). The acknowledgments mention two anonymous reviewers whose feedback improved the manuscript (p. 20), but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Whether the 5 m spacing and 5 Hz cutoff were fixed before inspecting the comparison is not stated (inference).

disagreements.target: Rayleigh integral modelling of SPE and other ground-motion infrasound (Jones et al. 2015; Blom et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: The paper argues the Rayleigh integral cannot handle topography or atmospheric refraction, but its own SPE-6 results show no noticeable difference from the Rayleigh integral at this low-relief site.
disagreements.quote: However, the Rayleigh integral is limited to a planar surface in a homogeneous medium.

disagreements.target: Finite-difference infrasound studies using single point sources (Kim and Lees 2011; Lacanna and Ripepe 2013; Fee et al. 2021 and [...]
disagreements.support: The piston benchmark shows a single point source cannot represent a source larger than the shortest wavelength; the distributed sources are offered instead.
disagreements.quote: acoustic sources are often oversimplified as [...] .

alternatives_considered.chosen: Air volume changes represented by distributed equivalent point sources
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Forcing boundary conditions on the surface; single point source
alternatives_considered.reason: Conventional point sources in finite-difference codes can be used, and propagation effects incorporated without modification
Finite difference accounts for topography and heterogeneous atmospheres

alternatives_considered.chosen: 1 m grid spacing for the piston benchmark (5 m, 13.6 ppw for SPE-6)
alternatives_considered.reason: Accuracy depends on points per wavelength; about 15 ppw keeps errors below 1%

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Higher frequency ranges (theory applies to any frequency)
alternatives_considered.reason: SPE-6 infrasound energy is mainly below 5 Hz; frequency range is limited by computing resources

alternatives_considered.chosen: Vertically layered atmosphere without lateral variation
alternatives_considered.reason: Coarse resolution of the GFS weather model

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both homogeneous and GFS vertically layered atmospheres
alternatives_considered.reason: Atmospheric effects are cumulative and may explain errors growing with distance
